story.headline: Trump says Board of Peace agrees Hamas disarmament
story.summary: Trump announced a Board of Peace framework for the complete disarmament of Hamas in Gaza, tied to phased Israeli withdrawal, but Hamas has not confirmed and only a 14-day plan to write the roadmap is agreed.
story.display_body: US President Donald Trump announced late on Thursday 30 July that his "Board of Peace" had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed factions in Gaza — a claim Hamas has not confirmed and that commits, for now, only to writing a roadmap. Trump called it a "HISTORIC" step toward peace; the framework says a detailed disarmament plan is to be prepared within 14 days, subject to sign-off by an international verification body, after which Hamas would hand weapons to a Palestinian National Committee while Israeli forces withdraw in step ("withdrawal must move in lockstep with decommissioning," said Board of Peace envoy Nickolay Mladenov). As of the announcement Hamas had not publicly agreed: negotiator Ghazi Hamad described it to Reuters as a "comprehensive framework" going beyond disarmament — one he said requires Israel to pull back to its October positions and increase aid — and warned Hamas would not implement any part if Israel fails to meet its obligations. No weapons have changed hands and no timeline for withdrawal is fixed.
story.why: A genuine, verified Hamas disarmament would be the biggest shift in the Gaza war to date, but on the evidence so far this is a US-announced framework awaiting both a written plan and the assent of the party expected to disarm — the gap between Trump's 'agreement reached' and Hamas's conditional, unconfirmed reading is the whole story.

story.headline: Russian missile hits NATO soil in Poland
story.summary: NATO said a Russian Kh-101 missile violated Polish airspace during an overnight barrage on Ukraine that killed at least 13, with Kyiv blaming a North Korean-supplied missile for a family's deaths near Kryvyi Rih.
story.display_body: A missile believed to be of Russian origin struck Polish (NATO) territory during an overnight barrage on Ukraine into Thursday 30 July, prompting Polish PM Donald Tusk to convene an emergency meeting. NATO said the projectile — which experts identified as a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile (a long-range, air-launched weapon) — violated Polish airspace and left a crater near Tarnawa-Kolonia in the country's east; Tusk stopped short of directly blaming Moscow pending investigation. The incursion came amid one of the war's larger salvos: roughly 70 missiles and 280 drones that killed at least 13 people across Ukraine, including a family near Kryvyi Rih. Kyiv says a North Korean-supplied ballistic missile destroyed that home, and President Volodymyr Zelensky blamed "untimely" and delayed Western air-defence deliveries for the deaths while renewing his appeal for more interceptors.
story.why: A Russian munition landing on the soil of a NATO member is the kind of incident that tests the alliance's response thresholds, and pairs an escalation risk with Kyiv's argument that thin air-defence stocks are now costing civilian lives.

story.headline: 40,000 migrants cross into Ceuta from Morocco
story.summary: More than 40,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Spain's enclave of Ceuta in 24 hours; at least nine died and Spain deployed the military.
story.display_body: More than 40,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta within 24 hours, and Madrid deployed the military to restore order after at least nine people died attempting the crossing. Spain's Interior Ministry gave the 40,000 figure on Friday 31 July after people rushed the frontier by sea and land; Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez travelled to the enclave. Ceuta authorities linked the surge to a Spanish Supreme Court ruling earlier in July that migrants arriving by sea cannot be summarily pushed back without due process — unlike those crossing by land — while relations with Rabat, which polices the border, remain a recurring pressure point. Troops were helping some who had entered irregularly return to Morocco.
story.why: Ceuta is one of the EU's only land borders with Africa, and a surge of this scale — far above the 'thousands' reported a day earlier — revives the question of how far Spanish-Moroccan cooperation, and EU asylum law, hold under a sudden crush.

story.headline: SNB posts CHF 25.2 billion first-half profit
story.summary: The Swiss National Bank reported a CHF 25.2 billion profit for the first half of 2026, driven by equity gains on foreign-currency positions and offset by a gold valuation loss.
story.display_body: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) reported a profit of CHF 25.2 billion for the first half of 2026, driven by gains on its foreign-currency stock portfolio and partly offset by a loss on gold. In interim results published Friday 31 July, the SNB said foreign-currency positions earned CHF 31.7 billion — including CHF 22.9 billion of price gains on equities — while a CHF 6.4 billion valuation loss was booked on gold (unchanged in volume, but down to CHF 104,812/kg at end-June from CHF 110,919 at end-2025). Swiss-franc positions added CHF 0.1 billion. The bank cautioned that its result swings with gold, currency and capital markets, so only "provisional conclusions" can be drawn about the full-year figure.
story.why: The SNB's profit determines whether the Confederation and the cantons receive their annual distribution — money that flows into public budgets — so a strong half-year, if it holds, eases a pressure point in federal-cantonal finances.

story.headline: Five charged over deadly Malley scaffold collapse
story.summary: Two years after a scaffold collapse killed three workers at Malley Phare in Prilly, five employees of the scaffolding firm have been formally charged.
story.display_body: Two years after a scaffold collapse killed three workers at the Malley Phare tower in Prilly (Vaud), five current or former employees of the scaffolding company have been formally charged (prevenus), with further charges possible. Le Temps reported Friday 31 July that the investigation into the 12 July 2024 collapse is tightening around the firm responsible for the scaffolding; being prevenu under Swiss procedure means formally suspected, not convicted.
story.why: It is the first concrete accountability step in one of Vaud's deadliest recent construction accidents, and signals the criminal probe is moving toward named defendants rather than the company alone.

story.headline: New Swiss laws take effect on 1 August
story.summary: From 1 August, Switzerland introduces littering fines up to CHF 300, a pension-ordinance fix for the 13th AHV payment, and a Sunrise mobile price rise.
story.display_body: A batch of Swiss rule changes takes effect on 1 August, the national holiday, touching household costs and pensions. New federal anti-littering rules allow fines of up to CHF 300 for dropping waste; an early amendment to the occupational-pension ordinance (BVV 2 — the rules governing second-pillar company pensions) prevents the new 13th AHV payment (the state old-age pension's added annual instalment) from pushing combined pensions over the 85%-of-final-salary cap and triggering cuts; and telecoms operator Sunrise raises most mobile and internet subscriptions by about CHF 1 a month. Airline Swiss also resumes Tel Aviv flights from 1 August, having repeatedly extended its suspension over the Iran-region tensions.
story.why: These are the small, dated rule changes that alter a household budget or a pension calculation in Switzerland from a fixed day — the kind of practical detail easy to miss until the bill or the payslip changes.
